questions.q: Per this lesson, what is a "security boundary"?
options: Any point in a system where the level of trust changes and a check has to run before the request can proceed
A physical wall around a company's data center
A field that has been encrypted with Shield Platform Encryption
The maximum number of API calls an org is allowed per day
questions.explain: A security boundary is a decision point where trust changes -- crossing it means a check has to run to confirm the access is actually allowed, not an assumption that it is.

questions.q: A user's profile grants Read access to the Account object in general. Which boundary determines whether they can see one specific Account record?
options: The org boundary
The record-sharing boundary (OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules)
The field-level boundary
The user/session boundary
questions.explain: Object-level CRUD permission (can they read Accounts at all) is a separate check from record-level sharing (can they read this specific Account) -- the record-sharing boundary, governed by OWD, role hierarchy, and sharing rules, decides the latter.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that an architect should name boundaries explicitly rather than treating "security" as one undifferentiated concern?
options: Because Salesforce requires a written list of boundaries before Shield can be purchased
Because only five boundaries are technically possible in any Salesforce org
Because each boundary needs its own deliberately designed control, and a failure at one boundary shouldn't automatically become a failure at the next one
Because naming boundaries removes the need for field-level security
questions.explain: Separating boundaries lets each one be defended independently, so that something like a phished login (crossing the org boundary) doesn't automatically expose every object, record, and field behind it -- that containment only works if each inner boundary was deliberately designed.

questions.q: Which of these correctly orders the boundaries from the outermost (org edge) to the innermost (a single piece of data)?
options: Field-level, record-sharing, CRUD, org
CRUD, field-level, org, record-sharing
Record-sharing, org, field-level, CRUD
Org, CRUD (object), record-sharing, field-level
questions.explain: The lesson lists the boundaries from outside in: the org boundary (login/network), then the object/CRUD boundary, then the per-record sharing boundary, then the innermost field-level boundary.

questions.q: A phishing attack successfully steals a sales rep's login credentials, and the attacker authenticates into the org. According to this lesson's reasoning, what determines whether the attacker can now read every Account and every sensitive field in the org?
options: Whether CRUD permissions, record-sharing rules, and field-level security were each independently configured correctly, since crossing one boundary doesn't automatically cross the next
Nothing -- successfully crossing the org boundary always grants full access to every record and field
Only whether the org has enabled login IP ranges
Only whether multi-factor authentication was required at login
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that a breach at the org boundary is contained by whatever independent controls exist at the inner boundaries -- if CRUD, sharing, and field-level security are all correctly configured, a stolen login still doesn't expose everything.
